subject: science
title: Forces and motion
description: Forces explained for ages 9 to 14: pushes and pulls, gravity and weight, friction, balanced and unbalanced forces, speed and magnets. Free practice with instant feedback.
intro: Why do things fall? Why does a bike stop when you brake? Forces are behind everything that moves. Follow the path and collect your stars.

units.title: What is a force?
units.blurb: Pushes, pulls, and what forces can do.

learn.p: A **force** is a push or a pull. You can't see a force, but you can see what it does. We draw forces as arrows: the arrow points the way the force acts.
A force can make something **start moving**, **speed up**, **slow down**, **stop**, **change direction** or **change shape** (like squashing a sponge).

Forces are measured in **newtons**, written **N**, named after the scientist Isaac Newton. You can measure a force with a **force meter** (also called a newton meter). It has a spring inside that stretches more when the pull is bigger.

questions.q: What is a force?
questions.hint: Think about what you do to a door to open or close it.
questions.explain: A force is a push or a pull. Opening a door is a pull or a push: a force.

questions.q: What unit are forces measured in?
questions.hint: The unit is named after a famous scientist.
questions.explain: Forces are measured in newtons (N), after Isaac Newton.

questions.q: Kicking a football is an example of a…
questions.hint: Does your foot move the ball away from you or towards you?
questions.explain: Your foot pushes the ball away from you, so it's a push.

questions.q: Opening a drawer towards you is an example of a…
questions.hint: Is the drawer coming towards you or going away?
questions.explain: You bring the drawer towards you, so it's a pull.

questions.q: Which of these can a force **not** do?
options: Change the colour of an object
Change the shape of an object
Change the direction an object is moving
questions.hint: Think about squashing, throwing and kicking. Which one is left over?
questions.explain: Forces can change how something moves and its shape, but pushing or pulling doesn't change its colour.

questions.q: Which tool do we use to measure a force?
questions.hint: Its other name is a newton meter.
questions.explain: A force meter (newton meter) measures forces in newtons. It has a spring that stretches more when the force is bigger.

questions.q: You squeeze a ball of modelling clay. What does the force change?
questions.hint: What does the clay look like after you squeeze it?
questions.explain: Squeezing changes the clay's shape. It is still the same clay, with the same colour.

questions.q: A ball is rolling along. A player heads it upwards. What does the force do to the ball?
options: It changes the direction the ball moves
questions.hint: Where was the ball going before, and where does it go after?
questions.explain: The push from the player's head changes the ball's direction, sending it upwards.

units.title: Gravity and weight
units.blurb: Why things fall, and the difference between mass and weight.

learn.p: **Gravity** is a pulling force. The Earth's gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth. That's why a dropped ball falls down.

**Mass** is how much matter (stuff) is in an object. It is measured in **kilograms (kg)**.
**Weight** is the force of gravity pulling on that mass. Weight is a force, so it is measured in **newtons (N)**.

On Earth, gravity pulls on every kilogram with a force of about **10 N** (more exactly 9.8 N). So:
**weight (N) = mass (kg) × 10**
A 3 kg bag weighs about 3 × 10 = 30 N.

The Moon's gravity is weaker: about 1.6 N for every kilogram. An astronaut's **mass** stays the same on the Moon, but their **weight** is about 6 times smaller. That's why astronauts can bounce so high!

questions.q: Which way does the Earth's gravity pull you?
options: Towards the centre of the Earth
It doesn't pull you at all
questions.hint: When you drop something, which way does it go?
questions.explain: Gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth, which we call "down".

questions.q: Mass is measured in…
questions.hint: You use this unit when you weigh flour for a cake.
questions.explain: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg). (Everyday scales say "weight", but they really measure mass.)

questions.q: Weight is measured in…
questions.hint: Weight is a force. What are forces measured in?
questions.explain: Weight is the force of gravity on an object, and forces are measured in newtons (N).

questions.q: Using 10 N for every kilogram, what is the weight of a 5 kg bag of potatoes on Earth?
questions.hint: weight = mass × 10

questions.q: A dog has a mass of 12 kg. What is its weight on Earth? (Use 10 N for every kg.)
questions.hint: Multiply the mass by 10.

questions.q: A suitcase weighs 200 N on Earth. What is its mass? (Use 10 N for every kg.)
questions.hint: This time go backwards: divide the weight by 10.
questions.explain: mass = weight ÷ 10 = 200 ÷ 10 = 20 kg.

questions.q: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. She travels to the Moon. What is her mass on the Moon?
questions.hint: Mass is the amount of stuff in her body. Does that change when she travels?
questions.explain: Her mass stays 70 kg: she is made of the same amount of stuff. Her **weight** is smaller on the Moon, because the Moon's gravity is weaker.

questions.q: On the Moon there is no air. An astronaut drops a hammer and a feather from the same height at the same time. What happens?
options: They land at the same time
questions.hint: On Earth, the feather is slowed down by air. What is missing on the Moon?
questions.explain: With no air resistance, everything falls at the same rate. Astronaut David Scott did this on the Moon in 1971, and they landed together.

units.title: Friction and air resistance
units.blurb: The forces that slow things down.

learn.p: **Friction** is a force between two surfaces that slide (or try to slide) over each other. It always acts **against** the movement.
Rough surfaces, like carpet or sandpaper, make **more** friction. Smooth surfaces, like ice, make **less** friction. That's why it's easy to slip on ice.

**Air resistance** and **water resistance** are kinds of friction. They push against things moving through air or water. **Streamlined** shapes, like a fish, a dolphin or a racing car, have less resistance.
Friction is useful: it lets your shoes grip the ground and lets brakes stop a bike. But it also slows machines down and wears things out, so we use oil and wheels to reduce it.

questions.q: A box is pushed to the right along the floor. Which way does friction act on the box?
options: To the left, against the movement
To the right, with the movement
questions.hint: Friction always tries to stop things sliding.
questions.explain: Friction acts against the movement. The box moves right, so friction acts to the left.

questions.q: A toy car is pushed with the same force on four surfaces. On which one will it roll the furthest?
questions.hint: Which surface is the smoothest?
questions.explain: Ice is the smoothest, so it gives the least friction. The car slows down least and goes furthest.

questions.q: Why do football boots have studs?
options: To increase friction so players don't slip
To reduce friction so players can slide
questions.hint: Think about running on wet grass.
questions.explain: Studs grip the ground and increase friction, so players don't slip when they run and turn.

questions.q: Which shape has the least air resistance when it moves?
questions.hint: Think about the shape of a racing car or a fast bird.
questions.explain: A streamlined shape lets air flow around it smoothly, so it has the least air resistance.

questions.q: Why does a parachute slow a skydiver down?
options: Its large surface causes a lot of air resistance
questions.hint: A parachute is very big. What does a big surface do as it moves through air?
questions.explain: The big canopy pushes against lots of air, making a large air resistance force upwards. Gravity still pulls, but the skydiver falls much more slowly.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of friction being **useful**?
options: The soles of shoes getting worn down
questions.hint: Which one is something we want to happen?
questions.explain: Brakes use friction to slow the wheels and stop the bike. The other two are friction being a nuisance.

questions.q: A bike chain is squeaky and stiff. What can you put on it to reduce friction?
questions.hint: What do mechanics use to make machine parts slide easily?
questions.explain: Oil makes the surfaces slippery, so they slide past each other with less friction.

questions.q: Why is a fish's body streamlined?
options: So there is less water resistance and it can swim easily
questions.hint: Think about which force acts against things moving through water.
questions.explain: A streamlined body lets water flow around it smoothly, so there is less water resistance.

units.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
units.blurb: Work out the resultant force and what happens next.

learn.p: When two forces are the **same size** and act in **opposite** directions, they are **balanced**. Balanced forces don't change how something moves: if it is still, it stays still; if it is moving, it keeps going at the **same speed** in the **same direction**.
If the forces are not balanced, there is a **resultant force**. An unbalanced force makes an object **speed up**, **slow down** or **change direction**.

Forces in **opposite** directions: take the smaller one away from the bigger one. 7 N to the right and 3 N to the left gives a resultant force of 7 − 3 = **4 N to the right**.
Forces in the **same** direction: add them together.
A floating boat has balanced forces. Its weight pulls it down, and the water pushes it up with the same size of force. This upward push is called **upthrust**.

questions.q: Are these forces balanced or unbalanced?
questions.hint: Are the two forces the same size? Do they point in opposite directions?
questions.explain: 5 N left and 5 N right are the same size and opposite, so they are balanced. The resultant force is 0 N.

questions.q: These are the only forces acting sideways on the box. What is the resultant force? Type the number of newtons.
questions.hint: The forces are opposite. Take the smaller from the bigger.
questions.explain: 8 N − 3 N = 5 N, to the right.

questions.q: Look at the same box. It starts still. Which way will it start to move?
questions.hint: Which way does the bigger force point?
questions.explain: The resultant force is 5 N to the right, so the box starts moving to the right.

questions.q: Two children push a heavy box in the same direction. One pushes with 30 N and the other with 20 N. What is the total (resultant) force from the two children? Type the number of newtons.
questions.hint: When forces point the same way, add them.

questions.q: A car is moving along a road. Its driving force is exactly the same size as the friction and air resistance against it. What happens to the car?
options: It keeps moving at the same speed
questions.hint: The forces are balanced. What do balanced forces do to something that is already moving?
questions.explain: Balanced forces don't change the motion. The car is already moving, so it keeps going at the same speed. (Many people think it must slow down, but it doesn't!)

questions.q: A boat is floating still on a lake. How does the upthrust compare with the boat's weight?
questions.hint: The boat is not moving up or down. Are the forces balanced?
questions.explain: The boat stays at the same level, so the forces are balanced: upthrust = weight.

questions.q: Tug of war! Team A pulls to the left with 500 N. Team B pulls to the right with 450 N. What is the resultant force? Type the number of newtons.
questions.hint: The teams pull in opposite directions.
questions.explain: 500 N − 450 N = 50 N, to the left.

questions.q: In that tug of war (Team A 500 N left, Team B 450 N right), which way does the rope move?
questions.hint: The resultant force is to the left. Which team is on the left?
questions.explain: The resultant force of 50 N is to the left, towards Team A, so Team A pulls the rope their way.

questions.q: A skydiver jumps out of a plane. At first, her weight is much bigger than the air resistance on her. What happens?
options: She falls at a steady speed
questions.hint: The forces are unbalanced, and the bigger force points down.
questions.explain: The resultant force is downwards, so she speeds up. As she gets faster, air resistance grows, until it balances her weight and she falls at a steady speed.

units.title: Speed
units.blurb: How fast? Use distance and time to find out.

learn.p: Speed tells you how far something travels in a certain time. A speed of 5 metres per second (**5 m/s**) means it travels 5 metres every second.

**speed = distance ÷ time**
A car that travels 100 m in 20 s has a speed of 100 ÷ 20 = **5 m/s**.

Distance in metres and time in seconds → speed in **m/s** (metres per second).
Distance in kilometres and time in hours → speed in **km/h** (kilometres per hour).

You can turn the formula around:
**distance = speed × time**
**time = distance ÷ speed**

questions.q: What is the speed of the runner? Type the number of metres per second.
questions.hint: speed = distance ÷ time

questions.q: A cyclist travels 150 m in 30 s. What is her speed?
questions.hint: Divide the distance by the time.

questions.q: A train travels 240 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.hint: Distance in km ÷ time in hours.
questions.explain: 240 ÷ 2 = 120 km/h. It's an average, because the train speeds up and slows down along the way.

questions.q: Which of these is a unit of speed?
questions.hint: Speed is a distance divided by a time.
questions.explain: m/s means metres per second: a distance divided by a time. kg is for mass, N is for force and m is for distance.

questions.q: A runner runs at 8 m/s for 10 s. How far does she run?
questions.hint: distance = speed × time

questions.q: A car travels at 30 m/s. How long does it take to travel 600 m?
questions.hint: time = distance ÷ speed

questions.q: Ali runs 100 m in 20 s. Ben runs 100 m in 16 s. Who is faster?
questions.hint: They run the same distance. Who takes less time?
questions.explain: Ben takes less time for the same distance, so he is faster. Ali: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s. Ben: 100 ÷ 16 = 6.25 m/s.

questions.q: Challenge: a cheetah can sprint 120 m in 4 s. What is its speed?
questions.hint: Divide 120 by 4.
questions.explain: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 m/s. That's over 100 km/h: cheetahs are the fastest land animals!

units.title: Magnets
units.blurb: Attract, repel, and which materials are magnetic.

learn.p: Magnets can push or pull some objects **without touching** them. A bar magnet has two ends called **poles**: a north pole (N) and a south pole (S).

**Opposite poles attract**: N and S pull together.
**Like poles repel**: N and N push apart, and so do S and S.

Only a few metals are magnetic: **iron**, **nickel** and **cobalt**, and **steel**, which is mostly iron. Most other metals, like aluminium, copper and gold, are **not** magnetic. Wood, plastic and glass are not magnetic either.
A compass needle is a tiny magnet. It points north because the Earth acts like a giant magnet. Recycling centres use huge magnets to pull steel cans out from aluminium cans.

questions.q: Will these two magnets attract or repel?
questions.hint: Look at the two poles that face each other in the middle.
questions.explain: The S pole of the first magnet faces the N pole of the second. Opposite poles attract.

questions.q: Will these two magnets attract or repel?
questions.hint: Which poles face each other in the middle?
questions.explain: S faces S. Like poles repel, so the magnets push apart.

questions.q: Will these two magnets attract or repel?
questions.hint: Look closely at the middle.
questions.explain: N faces N. Like poles repel.

questions.q: Which of these is attracted to a magnet?
questions.hint: Remember the magnetic metals: iron, nickel and cobalt.
questions.explain: Iron is magnetic, so the nail is attracted. Aluminium, plastic and wood are not magnetic.

questions.q: Which metal is **not** magnetic?
questions.hint: Three of these are the magnetic metals.
questions.explain: Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Aluminium is a metal, but it is not magnetic.

questions.q: Can a magnet attract a paper clip through a sheet of paper?
options: Yes: magnetic forces can act through thin materials like paper
No: the magnet has to touch the paper clip
questions.hint: Think about fridge magnets holding up a drawing.
questions.explain: Magnetic forces work without touching and can pass through thin materials like paper. That's how fridge magnets hold up pictures.

questions.q: A recycling centre uses a giant magnet to sort cans. Which cans does the magnet pick up?
questions.hint: Steel is mostly iron.
questions.explain: Steel contains iron, so steel cans are attracted. Aluminium cans are left behind.

questions.q: Why does a compass needle point north?
options: The Earth acts like a giant magnet, and the needle is a small magnet
questions.hint: What is a compass needle made of?
questions.explain: The needle is a small magnet. The Earth behaves like a giant magnet, so the needle lines up and points north.
